These annual meetings—often called conjoint conferences or June conferences—were held around the first of June each year in honor of Brigham Young’s birthday. (Susa Young Gates,History of the Young Ladies’ Mutual Improvement Association of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints[Salt Lake City: Deseret News, 1911], 140–142, 221–222.)

Latter-day Saint women began participating in missionary work soon after the church was organized, often informally. Some married women served missions with their husbands before 1898. (See “Women with a Mission: Series Introduction,” accessed May 24, 2016,history.lds.org; see also Carol Cornwall Madsen, “Mormon Missionary Wives in Nineteenth-Century Polynesia,” inProclamation to the People: Nineteenth-Century Mormonism and the Pacific Basin Frontier,ed. The first general Relief Society conference was held in 1889, and the organization continued to hold semiannual conferences until 1945. From 1945 to 1975, the Relief Society held only one conference per year, in September or October. That annual meeting was eventually replaced by today’s general women’s session. (Derr et al.,First Fifty Years,561–564; Jill Mulvay Derr, Janath Russell Cannon, and Maureen Ursenbach Beecher,Women of Covenant: The Story of Relief Society[Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1992], 378–379, 473n85; see alsoAppendixherein.)

In 1933, United States president Franklin D. Roosevelt popularized the notion of fireside chats with the first in a series of radio broadcasts by that name. The Latter-day Saint tradition of firesides began with Salt Lake Institute of Religion founder Lowell L. Bennion in 1935. Bennion invited students to join him for evening gospel discussions in a University Ward room that had a fireplace. (Douglas B. Craig,Fireside Politics: Radio and Political Culture in the United States, 1920–1940[Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2000], 83–89; Sheridan R. Sheffield, R. Scott Lloyd, and Mike Cannon, “Some Things Uniquely LDS,”Church News,Jan. 25, 1992.)
